Prop 45 would make major changes to CEQA. But many CEQA reformers don’t support it
By Joe Garofoli (https://www.sfchronicle.com/author/joe-garofoli/) , Political Columnist Oct 21, 2026
Key CEQA reformers are concerned that Prop 45 could lead to more suburban sprawl.
Santiago Mejia/S.F. Chronicle
Some California leaders who have spent years spearheading changes to the state’s landmark environmental protection law either haven’t taken a position on or are opposing Proposition 45, which would take even bigger chunks out of CEQA, the California Environmental Quality Act.
CEQA was created in 1970 under then-Gov. Ronald Reagan to protect the beauty and vibrancy of the state. It requires developers to disclose potential environmental impacts of their projects and work with communities to blunt those impacts. But for decades, the law has been weaponized to jam development by everyone from NIMBYs to construction unions to wealthy suburbanites. A 2024 study (https://lhc.ca.gov/wp-content/uploads/Report279.pdf) by the Little Hoover Commission found that on average, “litigation adds almost two years to project time frames. In the face of such lengthy delays, financing can vanish, stopping a project even if it would eventually have survived the CEQA process and been approved.” Preparing an environmental impact report can take a year or longer and cost up to $1 million.
Powerful labor interests have balked at changing CEQA, because unions have long used the law to extract wage concessions from developers. Wealthy suburbanites have used it to halt unwanted development. The same study found that 78% of CEQA litigation “may disproportionately challenge housing in higher-income neighborhoods.”
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Prop 45 — backed by the California Chamber of Commerce, local chambers around the state, developers and affordable housing advocates — seeks to expedite development by imposing strict deadlines on certain categories of infrastructure projects described as “essential”: housing, water, clean energy, healthcare, public safety, wildfire mitigation, broadband internet access, education and transportation.
Yet some key CEQA reformers are concerned about its unintended consequences, in particular that its provisions to loosen regulations could lead to more suburban sprawl — developments far from urban centers that destroy forest or agricultural land and force residents to drive everywhere, increasing air pollution and greenhouse gas emissions, and exacerbating the climate crisis. Infill housing, meanwhile, is denser and typically enables residents to walk or take public transit to work. Many of California’s leading CEQA reformers oppose suburban sprawl and advocate for infill development, particularly near public transit.
State Sen. Scott Wiener, D-San Francisco, one of the architects of some of the Legislature’s most consequential CEQA reforms over the past decade, isn’t taking a position on the measure. Neither is one of his top allies, California YIMBY (https://cayimby.org/blog/proposition-45-2026/), which advocates for building more homes to ease California’s crippling housing crisis. Environmental advocate Tom Steyer supported (https://x.com/TomSteyer/status/1942757810686812370?s=20) CEQA reforms crafted in the Legislature but opposes (https://tomsteyer.substack.com/p/my-california-ballot-guide) Prop 45. It “goes way beyond any common-sense reforms to CEQA and is using the law to circumvent the public process and due process,” he wrote on Substack.
Other top Democrats have ducked taking a position.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
On Monday, when a reporter asked (https://x.com/joegarofoli/status/2112263830495810011?s=20) Xavier Becerra, the Democratic candidate for governor, about Prop 45, he spent nearly a minute talking about his support for Proposition 1, on affordable-housing bonds, before saying he “hasn’t weighed in on a lot of the other initiatives.” He said nothing about Prop 45.
Gov. Gavin Newsom, who has signed several key CEQA reform measures, announced his position on 12 of the 14 measures on the Nov. 3 ballot (https://www.sfchronicle.com/politics/article/gavin-newsom-ballot-propositions-22470170.php), but not Props 45 or 42, one of two measures designed to invalidate Prop 40, the billionaire tax, if it passes.
Wiener told me he believes that CEQA is still in “serious need of reform.” And while he thinks Prop 45 “advances some very positive reforms like setting clear and firm timelines for permitting,” it also contains “problematic provisions like streamlining sprawl development.”
“As a result, I’m not taking a position on the measure,” he said.
Wiener is in a close race to succeed Speaker Emerita Nancy Pelosi in a San Francisco House race and may not want to further antagonize organized labor, which largely opposes Prop 45 and supports his opponent, Supervisor Connie Chan.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
California YIMBY is focused on infill development, and its leaders say Prop 45 does little to help those projects.
“The reason we have no position is because it’s not a pure-play housing thing,” Matthew Lewis, director of communications for California YIMBY, told me. “We are CEQA reformers for housing, and we reformed CEQA for housing” through legislation.
Likewise, SPUR, the San Francisco nonprofit think tank that has supported other CEQA reforms, stopped short (https://www.spur.org/voter-guide/2026-11/ca-prop-45-environmental-review-ceqa) of backing Proposition 45 because it “would make broader changes that conflict with SPUR’s vision for urban growth. The measure could accelerate desirable projects, such as infill housing near transit and zero-emission energy infrastructure, but it could also streamline development that contributes to sprawl or environmental harm, including subdivisions on the urban edge and polluting energy facilities,” the organization wrote of its position, which is “No recommendation.”
In a sign of how the measure has scrambled traditional party loyalties, Prop 45 has even split California Republicans, who have long complained about regulations slowing housing production. Steve Hilton, the GOP candidate for governor who advocates building 10 more California cities, largely through the construction of single-family homes in sprawl-like developments, has said supportive things about Prop 45 but hasn’t taken a position. The California Republican Party has endorsed (https://cagop.org/endorsements/) Prop 45, but half a dozen local Republican Party groups oppose it, including the Marin County Republican Party.
Marin County Republican Party Chairman John Turnacliff said his members are worried that Prop 45 could lead to “crony capitalism.”
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
“Let’s say some big data center developer comes in and takes care of some people in the Legislature with donations, and then all of a sudden they’re pushing for those guys to be qualified for this Proposition 45 benefit of not having to go through all the CEQA stuff, and then they get a fast-track deal,” Turnacliff said.
But other leading CEQA reformers are backing Prop 45, including Assembly Member Buffy Wicks, D-Oakland, who wrote (https://www.sfchronicle.com/politics/joegarofoli/article/california-ceqa-20244075.php?utm_campaign=CMS%20Sharing%20Tools%20(Premium)&utm_source=share-by-email&utm_medium=email) a bill signed by Newsom last year that exempted most infill housing projects from the environmental reviews required under CEQA.
“What Prop 45 represents is a thoughtful way to actually get the projects (completed) that are essential for our communities,” Wicks told reporters Monday at a housing-related campaign event for Becerra in El Cerrito. “It still requires (projects) to go through CEQA. It just puts important shot clocks on it.”
Housing Action Coalition, another frequent ally on CEQA reform legislation, is also breaking ranks to back Prop 45. The organization felt that there were gaps in some recent reform legislation in Sacramento — like the ability to quickly build housing on parking lots at dilapidated shopping mall sites — that weren’t covered by existing legislation, said Ali Sapirman, the group’s advocacy and policy manager. Even though the Housing Action Coalition typically doesn’t support legislation that could lead to sprawl, it is confident that existing CEQA laws could be used to stop unwanted sprawl projects.
“And those gaps are real in terms of numbers,” Sapirman said. “The permitting delays add more than $75,000 to the cost of a new home, and that was really critical to our members.”
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
But those gaps weren’t enough to convince other CEQA reformers to back Prop 45.
“There’s a bunch of stuff that 45 could do that we’re like, ‘Well, that would not be a great outcome,’” said California YIMBY’s Lewis. “But there’s some stuff that it would do that could be a good outcome. We weighed those against each other, and we were like, yeah, they kind of cancel each other out. We’re not going to weigh in on this one.”

Big Tech companies and California’s largest oil and gas well operator are spending millions to pass a ballot measure that would clear hurdles for industrial projects such as gas pipelines and possibly data centers.
Proposition 45 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop45-text-proposed-laws.pdf) would alter the California Environmental Quality Act, known as CEQA, which requires often time-consuming reviews and public input for infrastructure and other construction projects. Those requirements would be clipped if voters pass the proposition in November, making projects harder to stop or delay.
The half-century-old environmental law has come under scrutiny for slowing housing construction, among other complaints. Last year, the state Legislature passed and Gov. Gavin Newsom signed bills exempting housing (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billNavClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260AB130) in developed urban and suburban areas from the law and giving “advanced manufacturing (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billNavClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260SB131)” businesses a pass.
It wasn’t enough to speed along needed housing, clean energy and other projects, say the proposition’s backers. California needs Proposition 45 to further “cut bureaucratic red tape and unnecessary delays,” as the measure’s text puts it, and make the state more affordable.
But the initiative’s opponents say such appeals are disingenuous. Housing and clean energy have never been “the real agenda behind this ballot measure,” said Woody Little, a spokesperson for the No on Prop 45 campaign. “It’s always been about polluting projects they can get through under the guise of addressing the housing crisis.”
In addition to speeding up environmental reviews for housing, wastewater treatment plants and other facilities, the proposition would benefit businesses behind projects that capture climate-warming carbon dioxide pollution.
Among them is California Resources Corp., an oil company that has spent $1 million to promote Proposition 45. The firm owns thousands of oil wells in the state and is developing technology it says is capturing carbon dioxide (https://calmatters.org/environment/2026/08/california-resources-corporation-carbon-terra-vault/) from its Elk Hills natural-gas power plant in Kern County. The proposition excludes new oil and gas production from its provisions but includes carbon dioxide pipelines.
A network of political insiders and oil lobbyists has secured state incentives (https://capitalandmain.com/californias-net-zero-roadmap-is-being-shaped-by-regulators-turned-lobbyists) for carbon capture technology, mirroring industry efforts worldwide (https://projects.propublica.org/carbon-captured/). California’s anti-emissions plans for the next two decades lean heavily on transporting carbon dioxide, a volatile gas, through hundreds of miles of pipelines (https://capitalandmain.com/californias-carbon-deadline-is-approaching-meeting-it-will-take-hundreds-of-miles-of-pipelines) spanning urban and rural areas to be buried under the Central Valley. Yet as a solution for climate change, capturing carbon has failed (https://ieefa.org/ccs) at scale and will likely never succeed (https://projects.propublica.org/why-carbon-capture-cant-solve-climate-change/), an investigation by the nonprofit newsroom ProPublica found.
California Resources Corp. has expanded its political influence in recent years. It is lobbying the state Public Utilities Commission (https://docs.cpuc.ca.gov/PublishedDocs/Efile/G000/M614/K484/614484379.PDF) to apply clean-power funds to electricity generated from methane, a fossil fuel, if the exhaust is captured. It’s spending money on state legislative races, funding more than a dozen business-friendly Democrats (https://cal-access.sos.ca.gov/PDFGen/pdfgen.prg?filingid=3196648&amendid=0) known to stonewall environmental legislation. And it gave gubernatorial candidate Xavier Becerra, also a Democrat, more than any other politician this election cycle, contributing half a million dollars (https://cal-access.sos.ca.gov/PDFGen/pdfgen.prg?filingid=3152126&amendid=0) to his campaign in May.

Yet California Resources Corp.’s greatest spending during this election cycle has been devoted to Proposition 45. In December, a company subsidiary gave $500,000 to a committee of the California Chamber of Commerce, the initiative’s sponsor. (The Chamber now brands itself as CalChamber.) In August, California Resources Corp. gave another $500,000 directly to the Yes on 45 campaign.
The oil company may have played a role in other contributions to the campaign. A Chamber of Commerce committee lent $2 million to the Proposition 45 campaign in June. The chamber’s board of directors, which includes California Resources Corp. chief executive Francisco Leon, controls that spending.
Unlike carbon capture, AI data centers may or may not be expedited by Proposition 45. While the initiative applies to “essential broadband internet access” infrastructure, supporters (https://natlawreview.com/article/prop-45-does-not-cover-data-centers-heres-why) and opponents (https://contracostaherald.com/californias-top-land-use-attorneys-agree-prop-45-would-speed-data-center-construction/) of the measure disagree on what this means. But campaign records show companies with data center interests back the proposition.
That includes California Resources Corp., which partnered with the developer Beacon Data Centers to advance a 275-megawatt campus for the technology (https://grist.org/energy/a-solution-to-data-center-backlash-put-them-in-oil-fields/) using electricity from its Elk Hills plant.
Another company in the sector, Prologis, donated $500,000 for Proposition 45 via its Modern Infrastructure Alliance Action Fund. The company — whose Western regional president, Megan Creecy-Herman, is a Chamber of Commerce board member — is planning (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/08/28/tech-san-jose-data-center-ai-build-property-develop-real-estate-economy/) five data centers in San Jose. The Modern Infrastructure Alliance Action Fund’s disclosure form lists the law firm Nielsen Merksamer, which formed fake consumer groups (https://www.sfchronicle.com/politics/article/newsom-oil-regulations-california-18156243.php) to buy ads opposing oil refinery regulation in 2023, the San Francisco Chronicle found.
One Nielsen Merksamer partner, Kurt Oneto, describes himself as the “official proponent” of Proposition 45 and is also a member of the chamber’s board. A law firm representative didn’t return Capital & Main’s call seeking comment.
Other data center developers and AI boosters, including Google co-founder and centibillionaire Sergey Brin, spent $10 million through a committee called Building a Better California in support of Proposition 45. Nielsen Merksamer’s phone number is listed (https://cal-access.sos.ca.gov/Campaign/Committees/Detail.aspx?id=1486767&session=2025) as a contact for that committee.
Utilities that could benefit from faster approvals for transmission and distribution infrastructure, as well as methane gas capture projects (https://capitalandmain.com/how-a-california-dairy-methane-project-threatens-residents-air-and-water), also gave millions in support of Proposition 45.
Pacific Gas & Electric Co., which is developing mixed-use residential and data center projects in San Jose, gave $2.3 million to Yes on 45 through another committee managed by Nielsen Merksamer (https://cal-access.sos.ca.gov/Campaign/Committees/Detail.aspx?id=1492786&session=2025).
Edison International gave $2 million directly to Yes on 45, and its affiliate Southern California Edison Company sent (https://cal-access.sos.ca.gov/PDFGen/pdfgen.prg?filingid=3207286&amendid=0) another $2 million to CalChamber’s Business PAC. That committee donated $3.4 million to Yes on 45.
Sempra, whose companies include Southern California Gas Company and San Diego Gas & Electric, contributed (https://cal-access.sos.ca.gov/PDFGen/pdfgen.prg?filingid=3207809&amendid=0) $1 million to the California Building Industry Association Issues Committee Supporting Proposition 45.
More big spending is on the horizon in the final weeks before the midterm. In September, a committee backed (https://cal-access.sos.ca.gov/Campaign/Committees/Detail.aspx?id=1275549&view=received&page=*) by California Resources Corp., Chevron and other corporations, called Californians for Jobs and a Strong Economy, sent $500,000 to a new committee called Golden State Forward. The group’s registration form (https://cal-access.sos.ca.gov/PDFGen/pdfgen.prg?filingid=3195450&amendid=2) shows its officers include lawyers at Nielsen Merksamer. At publication time, its main beneficiaries (https://cal-access.sos.ca.gov/Campaign/Committees/Detail.aspx?id=1496179&view=late3) were Assembly candidates Eric Lucan in the Bay Area and David Penaloza in Orange County, both Democrats fending off more progressive challengers in tight races.

PROP
45
MODIFIES ENVIRONMENTAL REVIEW FOR CERTAIN PROJECTS. INITIATIVE STATUTE.
SUMMARY
Put on the Ballot by Petition Signatures
Amends California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA) to expedite environmental review for certain projects (including most housing, transportation, water, and health projects) by setting deadlines to complete environmental review and resolve lawsuits challenging project approvals. Fiscal Impact: Initial costs for state and local governments, likely in the high tens of millions of dollars—potentially exceeding $100 million—annually, partly covered by fees. Uncertain, potentially more significant positive or negative longer-term fiscal effects. Supporters: California Children’s Hospital Association; California Water Association; California Council for Affordable Housing Opponents: Coalition for Clean Air; CA Environmental Voters; Physicians for Social Responsibility, LA; National Wildlife Federation
WHAT YOUR VOTE MEANS
YES
A YES vote on this measure means: Certain public and private projects would be eligible for new project review and court challenge procedures. For example, new procedures would tighten time limits for environmental review and reduce the scope of what courts can consider when reviewing legal challenges.
NO
A NO vote on this measure means: Public and private projects would continue to use existing project review and court challenge procedures.
ARGUMENTS
PRO
The failing status quo is making California unaffordable. Prop. 45 fixes our broken system and lowers our high cost of living by cutting red tape to build housing, water, schools, hospitals, clean energy, and wildfire prevention faster—while maintaining California’s strong environmental protections. Vote YES for a more affordable California. YESonProp45.com
CON
PROPOSITION 45 LIMITS ENVIRONMENTAL AND PUBLIC REVIEW OF PROJECTS BUILT IN YOUR COMMUNITY. It guts The California Environmental Quality Act—flipping California law to protect corporate profits over public health and our air and water. Prop. 45 won’t lower your costs: its utility and corporate funders profit while taxpayers pay more. VOTE NO.

PROP
45
MODIFIES ENVIRONMENTAL REVIEW FOR CERTAIN PROJECTS. INITIATIVE STATUTE.
ANALYSIS BY THE LEGISLATIVE ANALYST
BACKGROUND
State Law Requires Government Agencies to Review the Environmental Impacts of Proposed Projects. State and local government agencies are responsible for reviewing and approving certain projects before they can be built. As part of this process, the California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA) requires an agency to consider how a project might negatively affect the environment before approving it. CEQA applies to many types of public and private projects, such as housing developments, school facilities, and highway expansions. Some exceptions apply. For example, state law exempts certain housing developments located near public transit from needing a CEQA review.
How the CEQA Process Works. The government agency first determines if CEQA applies to a project. If so, it then determines if the project could significantly affect the environment and if those impacts could be avoided or reduced with minor changes to the project. If making minor changes cannot avoid or reduce significant impacts, the agency must do a more detailed review called an environmental impact report (EIR). (The majority of projects do not require an EIR; however, EIRs are somewhat more common for large and complex projects.) The EIR analyzes possible environmental impacts the project could cause and considers alternatives that could reduce those impacts. After finishing the environmental review, the agency decides whether to approve the project. At certain times during this process, the government agency must seek and consider comments about the project’s environmental review from the public and other government agencies.
People Can Sue the Government Agency About Its CEQA Review. After a government agency has completed the CEQA review and decided whether to approve a project, people who think the agency did not follow the CEQA process correctly can sue the agency. For example, a project opponent might argue that the environmental analysis was inadequate. If the court finds that the agency did not follow CEQA correctly, it can stop the whole project and require the agency to fix the part of the process that was problematic.
Many Projects Also Need to Get Other Approvals. Besides CEQA review, many projects need approval or permits from other local and/or state government agencies before they can proceed. For example, a business that wants to build a health clinic might need the local government to change land use rules before it can proceed. It also may need state agencies to review and approve how the project might affect certain wildlife species and water quality.
PROPOSAL
Proposition 45 creates new procedures for reviewing certain types of projects that it defines as “essential.” Figure 1 lists the types of projects eligible for the new procedures. The proposition (1) tightens time limits for CEQA review, permits, and court challenges; (2) changes parts of the CEQA review process; and (3) changes the court’s review process for CEQA lawsuits. The proposition gives eligible project applicants the option of using the new procedures or existing procedures.
Tightens Time Limits for Review and Court Challenges of Eligible Projects. Proposition 45 creates more binding time limits for state and local governments to do both CEQA and permitting reviews. This includes time limits for determining if a project application is complete, finishing the EIR, and granting other types of approvals and permits. For example, Proposition 45 allows an applicant to request an agency hearing- and potentially file a lawsuit with the courts-if an agency does not meet the 365-business-day time limit for finishing the EIR. The proposition also creates a time limit for courts to resolve legal challenges.
Changes CEQA Review for Eligible Projects. For eligible projects, Proposition 45 makes several changes to the CEQA review process, including:
Application Process. Requires the government agency to specify all information that must be included in an application before it is submitted. (Current law allows agencies to repeatedly request additional information or project changes.)
How Environmental Impacts Are Assessed. Requires the agency to assess potential environmental impacts based on the laws and standards in place at the time the project application is submitted. (Current law lets the agency consider new information and revise its review standards when doing the EIR.)
Project Alternatives. Allows the applicant to develop only one project alternative for the agency to consider. (Current law requires the agency-not the applicant-to develop and consider multiple project alternatives that could reduce environmental impacts.)
Consultation With Native Tribes. Requires the agency and applicant to consult about the project only with California native tribes that have been formally recognized by the federal government. (Current law requires consultation with a wider range of tribes.)
Public Comment Periods. Limits how long the agency can accept comments from the public and other government agencies about the project. (Current law sets a minimum number of days-not a maximum-for public review.)
Changes How Courts Review Challenges to Eligible Projects. Proposition 45 makes several changes to the court’s review process when someone challenges a government agency’s approval of an eligible project. For example, it reduces the scope of what the court can consider in CEQA lawsuits. The proposition also prevents the court from stopping the whole project if it finds that the agency did not follow CEQA correctly. Instead, the court can only stop the part of the project where the environmental review did not comply with CEQA while the agency fixes the problem.
FISCAL EFFECTS
Initial Costs for State and Local Governments. During the first several years, Proposition 45 likely would increase costs for the state and local governments, including state courts. These costs likely would be in the high tens of millions of dollars annually, potentially exceeding $100 million annually . For example, state and local governments would have costs to develop new guidelines and standards for reviewing eligible projects’ environmental impacts, meet tighter time limits, and address court challenges. Fees paid by project applicants and people filing lawsuits would cover some of these costs. After this initial period, while some costs could continue, others likely would decline over time. For example, the changes to how courts can review CEQA lawsuits could mean fewer people will sue in the future, which could reduce costs for agencies and state courts in the long term.
In the Longer Term, Uncertain but Potentially More Significant Fiscal Effects. Proposition 45’s changes to project review and court challenge procedures for eligible projects could have various fiscal effects for state and local governments. The overall fiscal effect of these changes-positive or negative-is uncertain but could be more substantial than the near-term effects. For example, two effects that could have significant but uncertain impacts are:
More Projects and Faster Timing. To the degree that Proposition 45’s changes to project review and court challenge procedures lead to eligible public projects being constructed more quickly, state and local governments likely would have lower project costs. Additionally, if the proposition’s changes result in more projects being completed overall, it could lead to an increase in tax revenues, such as from property taxes.
Negative Environmental Impacts. To the degree that Proposition 45’s changes to project review and court challenge procedures lead to approval of projects with negative environmental impacts that would not have otherwise occurred, government agencies could face higher costs to respond to those impacts.

PROP
45
MODIFIES ENVIRONMENTAL REVIEW FOR CERTAIN PROJECTS. INITIATIVE STATUTE.
ARGUMENT IN FAVOR OF PROPOSITION 45
LENGTHY DELAYS AND RED TAPE ARE BLOCKING ESSENTIAL PROJECTS & DRIVING UP OUR COST OF LIVING.
Families cannot afford to live in California because we are failing to deliver the basics. California’s outdated system for approving essential housing, water, clean energy, roads, schools, hospitals, and wildfire prevention projects is too slow, too bureaucratic, and too costly—driving up the cost of living for everyone.
Endless delays, red tape, and frivolous lawsuits make life more expensive and block the projects Californians need—driving up costs for housing, electricity, and water; wasting taxpayer dollars; worsening wildfire risk; increasing traffic; overcrowding schools; and delaying hospital and infrastructure upgrades.
PROP. 45 LOWERS OUR HIGH COST OF LIVING BY MAKING IT FASTER & LESS EXPENSIVE TO BUILD ESSENTIAL PROJECTS.
Prop. 45 streamlines approvals by setting enforceable timelines for project approvals; requires courts and government agencies to base decisions on the laws and regulations in place when the project application is submitted; and creates a faster, more predictable process for legal challenges while reducing frivolous lawsuits.
PROP. 45 STREAMLINES CALIFORNIA’S MOST-PRESSING ESSENTIAL PROJECTS, INCLUDING:
• Water quality and supply projects • Hospitals and healthcare facilities • Housing, including homes and apartments • Wildfire prevention • Schools and classrooms • Roads, bridges and transit • Clean energy and electric grid reliability infrastructure
PROP. 45 WILL:
REDUCE THE COST OF HOUSING. Permitting delays add more than $75,000 to the cost of a new home. Prop. 45 will help lower rents and mortgages and save families tens of thousands of dollars on a home purchase.
LOWER ELECTRICITY COSTS. Delays in building clean energy and electric grid infrastructure drive up electricity costs for working families. Prop. 45 helps lower electricity costs.
PROTECT TAXPAYERS. Lengthy delays drive massive cost overruns on public projects—roads, schools, hospitals, water systems, and wildfire prevention—costing taxpayers billions more. Prop. 45 cuts costly delays, reduces costs, and helps keep projects on time and on budget.
CREATE GOOD-PAYING JOBS AND STRENGTHEN OUR ECONOMY. Prop. 45 will create tens of thousands of good-paying jobs and billions in economic activity.
PROP. 45 MAINTAINS CALIFORNIA’S STRONGEST-IN-THE-NATION ENVIRONMENTAL PROTECTIONS.
California should not have to choose between protecting the environment and building the essential projects we need. Under Prop. 45, projects must comply with all of California strong environmental laws protecting our air, water, wildlife, and health. Prop. 45 does not exempt a single project from environmental review.
PROP. 45 PROTECTS COMMUNITY INPUT AND LOCAL DECISION MAKING.
Under Prop. 45, cities and counties retain full authority to approve or deny projects, and residents keep a meaningful voice in decisions affecting their communities.
AFFORDABLE HOUSING ADVOCATES, HEALTHCARE PROFESSIONALS, EDUCATORS, WATER PROVIDERS, CLEAN ENERGY LEADERS AND CIVIL RIGHTS LEADERS SUPPORT PROP. 45.
Prop. 45 is supported by a broad coalition of organizations, including:
• American Clean Power—California • California League of United Latin American Citizens (LULAC) • NAACP California/Hawaii State Conference • California Taxpayers Association • Environmental Policy Innovation Center
YES ON PROP. 45 TO BUILD A MORE AFFORDABLE CALIFORNIA.
Every year of delay means Californians wait longer and pay more for the essential projects we need. It’s time to cut red tape, protect our environment and build the projects California needs to make life more affordable.
VOTE YES ON PROP. 45.
YESonProp45.com
Ann-Louise Kuhns , President
California Children’s Hospital Association
Jennifer Capitolo , Executive Director
California Water Association
Jenna Abbott , Executive Director
California Council on Affordable Housing
REBUTTAL TO ARGUMENT IN FAVOR OF PROPOSITION 45
PROPOSITION 45 WON’T LOWER YOUR COSTS.
It doesn’t require a single project to lower your rent, your mortgage, or your utility bills. 45’s corporate funders profit while you bear the cost of their pollution.
PROP. 45 DOESN’T DELIVER AN AFFORDABLE CALIFORNIA. IT LIMITS ENVIRONMENTAL AND PUBLIC REVIEW AND RISKS PUBLIC HEALTH.
Prop. 45 could have been about building what California needs. It isn’t. Funded by gas and electric utilities and corporate PACs, Prop. 45 cuts their costs, not yours. Prop. 45 flips California law to protect their projects, harming public health and our air and water.
PROP. 45 PUTS YOUR HEALTH AT RISK AND STICKS YOU WITH THE BILL. Weaker environmental review means more pollution near homes and schools, more asthma and more emergency-room visits. When polluters don’t clean up, taxpayers and ratepayers pay more to cover the costs.
PROP. 45 TAKES AWAY PUBLIC INPUT. It limits the environmental review of new projects and your right to provide input and be heard. 45 even gives developers new rights to challenge cities and counties, while making it more difficult for project opponents to successfully challenge an agency’s decision.
Prop. 45 rewrites the rules that govern how California protects its citizens from the harm caused by major developments. Prop. 45 weakens environmental safeguards and radically shifts power to corporate polluters.
Protect your air quality, your drinking water, your family’s health, your tax dollars, and your right to be heard.
Join nurses, community and public health advocates.
VOTE NO ON PROP. 45.
www.NoProp45CA.com
Chris Tarver , R.N., President
American Nurses Association, CA
Vanessa Forsythe , RN
California Nurses for Environmental Health and Justice
Martha Arguello , Executive Director
Physicians for Social Responsibility, LA
ARGUMENT AGAINST PROPOSITION 45
PROPOSITION 45 LIMITS ENVIRONMENTAL AND PUBLIC REVIEW OF PROJECTS BUILT IN YOUR COMMUNITY. VOTE NO ON PROP. 45 TO PROTECT WATER, AIR QUALITY AND PUBLIC HEALTH.
Proposition 45 limits both the environmental review of major new development projects and the public’s right to be heard. Prop. 45 lets projects move forward with far less scrutiny of their harms to air, water and public health.
PROP. 45 WEAKENS CRITICAL PROTECTIONS FOR AIR AND WATER QUALITY BY GUTTING THE CALIFORNIA ENVIRONMENTAL QUALITY ACT (CEQA).
CEQA is California’s most important air and water quality protection law. It requires public agencies to identify, publicly disclose, and consider reducing harm to air, water, and wildlife before approving projects. Prop. 45 eliminates many of CEQA’s existing protections— letting developers fast-track the polluting projects you don’t want next door, with fewer protections for the water you drink and air you breathe.
PROP. 45 CUTS THE PUBLIC OUT OF DECISIONS THAT AFFECT YOUR FAMILY.
Today, you have a voice in what’s built near you and your family. Prop. 45 reduces public agency requirements to consider public comments on proposed projects—comments that often expose potential contamination of air and water, and damage to our coast, rivers, and wildlife. If Prop. 45 passes, decisions about what gets built near your home, your children’s school, and your water supply would be made with less information and less public input. Prop. 45 reduces your ability to protect your family and community from harm.
We need CEQA’s protections more than ever since federal protections have been weakened.
THEY POLLUTE. YOU PAY.
The nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office warns Prop. 45 could approve projects that result in “unintended negative environmental impacts.” When corporations aren’t required to reduce their pollution, taxpayers get stuck paying to clean up cancer-causing chemicals from our drinking water and contaminated lands.
PROP. 45 WON’T LOWER YOUR COSTS.
Prop. 45 doesn’t include any requirement to lower your housing costs or your utility bills. The corporations paying for Prop. 45 will profit while you keep paying.
WHO’S BEHIND PROP. 45?
Prop. 45 was written by the California Chamber of Commerce and financed by gas and electric utilities and corporate PACs. It gives the polluters and corporations funding Prop. 45 greater freedom to put whatever they want next to your home. Your family’s health and environmental quality are more important than corporate profits.
JOIN A BROAD COALITION OF PUBLIC HEALTH, ENVIRONMENTAL, AND COMMUNITY GROUPS OPPOSING PROP. 45, INCLUDING:
• National Wildlife Federation • California Communities Against Toxics • California Environmental Voters • California Environmental Justice Alliance • California Nurses for Environmental Health & Justice • Clean Water Action • Coalition for Clean Air • Physicians for Social Responsibility—Los Angeles
Whether you’re a Democrat, a Republican, or an independent, vote NO on Prop. 45 to protect your air and water, your tax dollars, and your right to be heard.
VOTE NO on Prop. 45.
www.NoProp45CA.com .
Joe Lyou , President
Coalition for Clean Air
Jennifer Clary , California Director
Clean Water Action
Matt Abularach-Macias , Political Director
California Environmental Voters
REBUTTAL TO ARGUMENT AGAINST
PROPOSITION 45
PROP. 45 IS THE CHANGE WE NEED TO BUILD A MORE AFFORDABLE CALIFORNIA.
The status quo is failing California. Families cannot afford to live here because we’re failing to deliver the basics. Endless delays, lawsuits and red tape are driving up the cost of essentials—housing, water, electricity, schools, roads, healthcare and wildfire protection.
We have a choice: accept the failing status quo—or fix it. PROP. 45 FIXES OUR BROKEN PROJECT APPROVAL SYSTEM by eliminating unnecessary delays for essential projects—lowering our cost of living and improving our quality of life.
PROP. 45’s OPPONENTS ARE MISLEADING VOTERS TO PROTECT THE BROKEN STATUS QUO.
The same opponents fighting Prop. 45 have spent decades using these same scare tactics to block even modest reforms. They’re fighting to preserve the broken status quo that’s making California unaffordable and lowering our quality of life.
WE DON’T HAVE TO CHOOSE BETWEEN PROTECTING THE ENVIRONMENT AND BUILDING ESSENTIAL PROJECTS.
FACT: Prop. 45 maintains every federal, state and local environmental law protecting our air, water, wildlife, and public health, including the Clean Air Act and Clean Water Act.
FACT: Prop. 45 does not eliminate a single environmental law or exempt a single project from environmental review.
FACT: Communities keep their voice. Residents maintain their right to provide public comments, oppose projects, and sue to stop projects.
FACT: Prop. 45 only applies to essential projects : water, hospitals, housing, schools, roads, transit, clean energy, and wildfire prevention.
THE CHOICE IS SIMPLE: accept the broken status quo—or fix it.
VOTE YES ON PROP. 45 TO BUILD A MORE AFFORDABLE CALIFORNIA.
Ann-Louise Kuhns , President
California Children’s Hospital Association
Ruben Grijalva , Former California State Fire Marshal
CAL FIRE
Robert Rivinius , President
Family Business Association of California

## The measure has important implications for projects in San Diego, where it routinely takes several years for large developments to navigate the environmental review process or survive legal challenges
Placed on the November ballot by the California Chamber of Commerce, Proposition 45 seeks to amend the California Environmental Quality Act with new procedures for the environmental review of projects defined as essential.
The state law, enacted in 1970, requires public agencies to study and disclose the environmental impacts of projects before approval.
The proposition, if approved by voters, would allow project applicants to opt into a revised CEQA process that includes tighter, enforceable timelines for permitting and review periods, shorter windows for public input and changes to how courts consider legal challenges.
Specifically, public agencies would be required to certify final environmental impact reports within 365 business days.
Today, agencies have a one-year timeline to complete the reports, but the deadline is not strictly enforced.
The proposition would allow project applicants to compel agencies to finish the work and schedule a hearing on a project decision if there is a delay.

Prop 45 explained: CEQA overhaul could shift who holds power over building
by
Alejandra Reyes-Velarde (https://calmatters.org/author/alejandra-reyesvelarde/)

IN SUMMARY
Prop 45 would set deadlines on environmental reviews and lawsuits for projects like housing, roads and water systems.
It would shift power toward the people proposing those projects.
That includes public agencies building their own.

In 2014, residents and environmental groups argued in a lawsuit that a California Department of Transportation road project planned to run through Richardson Grove State Park failed to properly evaluate how it could harm the redwood trees. It still took courts a total of 15 years to resolve all of the related legal complaints before Caltrans could move forward with building.
Environmental advocates say the litigation led to changes that better protect redwood trees. But pro-building advocates point to the case as evidence that the California Environmental Quality Act and the review process it requires need an overhaul.
Proposition 45 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-45-environmental-review/) , a November ballot initiative that aims to streamline the process, would change how fights like this one play out.
At the heart of the debate over the measure is who holds power over environmental reviews. Some legal experts say Prop. 45 would shift power away from courts and the public, giving project applicants, who include developers and public agencies building their own projects, more control at key points. For public agencies, including cities, counties and state entities, it’s complicated: an agency could lose discretion when it reviews someone else’s project and gain speed and certainty when it builds its own.
The California Chamber of Commerce, the measure’s sponsor, says the measure would cut costs by speeding up building. Critics say it goes much further than streamlining.
“This is not surgical at all,” said Ethan Elkind, a climate law expert at the Berkeley School of Law. “This would be a sea change.”
How does CEQA work?
California’s landmark environmental review law, signed in 1970, requires agencies to take into account the environmental impacts of a development and help avoid them.
Over decades, developers have raised concerns about the process, arguing litigation and bureaucracy slow down needed housing. Environmental groups say it gives communities a say in how projects get built.
In response to a housing shortage and high prices, state leaders have moved to ease CEQA’s reach over housing. Most recently, in 2025, Gov. Gavin Newsom signed laws that exempt many housing (https://calmatters.org/housing/2025/06/ceqa-urban-development-infill-budget/) projects from having to go through a lengthy environmental review process.
Prop. 45 would reach housing that doesn’t qualify for those exemptions, along with roads, water and other infrastructure projects.
Contractors with PG&E work in a trench to lay underground electric cables in Placer County on Oct. 17, 2024. Photo by Miguel Gutierrez Jr., CalMatters
Under the current process, public agencies are responsible for reviewing the potential environmental impacts of projects. Project applicants, usually developers, present an initial study summarizing the expected impacts. The lead public agency overseeing the review decides whether the impacts are significant enough to warrant more thorough scrutiny.

Public agencies are responsible for comparing the effects of a range of project alternatives, including a “no project” scenario.
Agencies judge project impacts using environmental standards they choose, covering everything from noise to air pollution, and they can revise those standards as new information emerges.
The public can then submit comments and suggest project alternatives, which the lead agency must consider. Members of the public, environmental groups and other stakeholders can sue to challenge reviews they think are illegal or incomplete.
Prop. 45 would give agencies 365 business days to decide on an environmental impact report for projects the measure defines as essential, including housing, roads, water, broadband and wildfire mitigation, and require courts to resolve cases within 270 calendar days.
Eligible applicants could choose the new procedures or stay with the existing ones.
What supporters and opponents say
Supporters of Prop. 45 say that the current process causes unnecessary delays and expenses, (https://www.hklaw.com/-/media/files/insights/publications/2026/09/hernandez_2026ceqastudy.pdf) including the costs of reviewing late public comments and defending against litigation.
Jennifer Barrera, chief executive of the California Chamber of Commerce, said the delays are costly.
“Time is money, and the delays that we see with regards to all of the red tape and bureaucracy … it could be anywhere from six to 10 years added on to the determination of moving a project forward,” Barrera said. “All those costs are ultimately borne by the consumers.”
Dan Dunmoyer, chief executive of the California Building Industry Association, said the proposition would decrease the cost of the average home by $75,000.
“If we want to have a society where people can live and thrive, we’ve got to find the sweet spot, and we think Prop. 45 is the sweet spot,” Dunmoyer said.
Opponents — a coalition that includes environmental groups, some labor unions and the California Democratic Party — say the measure goes far beyond basic streamlining, and gives project applicants too much power, undercutting the point of CEQA. They say Prop. 45 would strip agencies of the tools they have to protect communities, increase costly litigation and practically eliminate agencies’ ability to enforce the law.
“When you’re undoing or undermining environmental review, or saying you don’t need to do as much environmental review, you can have less community input for a project,” said Aruna Prabhala, an attorney for the Center for Biological Diversity who works on the opposition campaign.
A power shift?
Prop. 45 doesn’t just make the process go faster. It also changes (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=45&year=2026) the rules for project applicants and the government agencies overseeing the review process, according to the Legislative Analyst’s Office, the Legislature’s nonpartisan adviser.
Applicants could choose just one project alternative for the agency to consider rather than the multiple alternatives agencies assess today. Agencies would have to judge a project’s impacts under the standards in place when the applicant applies, rather than revising them as new information emerges, and list everything an application requires up front. If an agency misses the 365-business-day deadline, the applicant could request a hearing and potentially sue.
The public and courts would have less say. Public comments would be subject to a strict 45-day deadline, and any late comments can’t be entered into the record that a judge could review if there’s litigation.
Courts could still order agencies to fix flawed reviews, but could stop only the part of a project that failed to comply, not the whole project.
Traffic flows past construction work on eastbound Highway 50 in Sacramento on Aug. 12, 2021. Photo by Rich Pedroncelli, AP Photo
The same rules would apply when public agencies are developers themselves. Agencies building roads or water systems, for instance, would have the option of just analyzing one project alternative and choosing the environmental rules that apply at the time of submission. If they’re sued and a court finds they made a mistake with just one piece of their review, the overall project could still move forward.
Sean Marciniak, an attorney for Hanson Bridgett, which helped the California Chamber of Commerce write the measure, said agencies would keep the power to reject projects and the measure would not override other planning or zoning laws.
“This will protect agencies in their decisions,” he said.
Why a county group is sitting this out
Organizations that represent local governments in California, including the League of California Cities and the California State Association of Counties, have mostly stayed out of the debate.
California’s rural counties say they have a problem with building housing, and they’ve historically advocated for CEQA reform.
These counties often have small populations. They’re strapped for cash and the staff needed to handle the complicated process, said John Kennedy, a policy advocate for the Rural County Representatives of California.
So when the California Chamber of Commerce proposed a ballot initiative to speed up environmental reviews, Prop. 45 at first looked like a natural fit.
“CEQA has long been misused and manipulated by a number of interest groups seeking to extract their own interests,” Kennedy said.
But the group, which represents parts of 40 counties, is sitting this one out. Its leaders voted to stay neutral; Kennedy said he suggested the group oppose it because he thinks it goes too far.
“Prop. 45 really puts the power in the hands of the project proponents, project developers, and limits local authority to require consideration of alternatives,” he said.
He worries local agencies would lose control over the standards that decide when noise, dust or runoff is significant enough to require action.
What Prop. 45 would have changed
In Richardson Grove, had the Caltrans case come up after Prop. 45, Caltrans could have benefited from a 270-calendar-day time limit on courts to resolve the case. If a court found a flaw, it could stop only the part of the project that fell short.
The case, Marciniak said, also shows how Caltrans could have used existing standards to make the review go more smoothly and quickly. In 2014, an appeals court found Caltrans’ environmental report applied no standard for judging harm to the redwoods’ roots, and noted a state parks handbook with guidelines for protecting trees from construction damage. “There are easy tweaks any agency can make to crystallize meaningful thresholds of significance,” he said.
Opponents say the case is not typical. It’s rare for a case to take so long, said Doug Carstens, an attorney who often represents environmental groups in CEQA cases. The fixes courts required made the review better, he added.
“In this instance you’re talking about trees, but Prop. 45 could also apply to an instance where there’s people,” Carstens said. “It’s a question of going too far.”
What would it cost, and what would it save
New housing construction in the Crocker Village neighborhood in Sacramento on Feb. 10, 2022. Photo by Miguel Gutierrez Jr., CalMatters
The measure’s backers pitch it as an answer to California’s cost-of-living crisis.
Amelia Matier, a spokesperson for the Prop. 45 campaign, said faster, more predictable reviews would let California build housing and infrastructure at lower cost.
A study by Blue Sky Consulting Group, commissioned by the California Chamber of Commerce, estimates state and local governments and other public agencies would see $1.5 billion in combined savings and additional revenues.
The Legislative Analyst’s Office estimates that state and local governments and courts would face initial costs in the high tens of millions of dollars annually, potentially more than $100 million, over the first several years, partly covered by fees.
Some costs would likely decline over time, the office said, but long-term impacts are unclear. For instance, faster building would likely lower project costs, but any harmful environmental impacts resulting from quicker reviews would cost state and local agencies more.
Carstens said the savings aren’t even guaranteed, and that the Chamber of Commerce is using the affordability debate to deregulate in favor of business.
“They say it’s about affordable housing, but that’s not anywhere visible in this measure,” Carstens said. “There’s no affordability provision or requirement for addressing the needs of people who are impoverished and underprivileged.”
If Prop. 45 passes, much would be left to the courts. The measure says it should be interpreted to give “the fullest possible weight” to approving and building essential projects. Opponents say that would tilt unclear language in favor of applicants.
Marciniak said the provision is meant for situations the authors couldn’t predict.
“There is going to be confusion, but I think importantly, a judge in California is going to look at this and understand immediately what it means,” he said.

Powerful Interests Aim to Weaken California’s Landmark Environmental Law
Utilities, developers and technology companies have spent tens of millions to pass Prop 45, which fast-tracks “essential” projects by limiting public and environmental review.

Political action committees funded by technology companies, the state’s major utilities and other corporate interests have spent several million dollars more to pass a ballot measure that would greenlight major development projects with minimal environmental or public review than public interest and labor groups have spent opposing it.
Developers and other corporate interests aim to streamline the California Environmental Quality Act, or CEQA (https://www.califaep.org/docs/CEQA_Handbook_2023_final.pdf), which requires public agencies to identify, disclose and mitigate a development project’s negative impacts on a wide range of environmental resources, including wildlife, air and water quality and tribal cultural resources.
Proposition 45 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop45-text-proposed-laws.pdf) shifts who determines the scope of environmental review from public agencies and communities to project developers by rewriting the state’s foundational environmental law to fast-track major projects.
Supporters of Prop 45, sponsored by the California Chamber of Commerce, have spent at least $36 million to pass the measure, the most recent state records show. Opponents, led by a coalition of more than 550 labor, health and environmental organizations, have spent about $30 million to defeat what they say will give polluters a free pass.

“Prop 45 will modernize the approval process for essential projects by establishing clear, enforceable timelines for agency decisions and court challenges,” the chamber said in promotional materials, “while keeping environmental protections intact and preserving worker protections, tribal protections and local control.”
Critics say Prop 45 will gut the state’s primary vehicle for allowing people to learn about plans for polluting developments in their neighborhoods and propose alternatives.
“It undermines basically every stage of that process,” said Woody Little, the spokesperson for No on Prop 45.
Little and his allies say the 41-page ballot measure (https://oag.ca.gov/system/files/initiatives/pdfs/25-0023A1%20%28%26quot%3BEssential%20Projects%26quot%3B%29.pdf) was written by corporations who have paid to get their special interests on the ballot to create loopholes that favor polluting industries like recently regulated (https://www.gov.ca.gov/2026/09/21/governor-newsom-signs-most-comprehensive-data-center-laws-in-the-nation-providing-communities-more-control-on-water-electricity-and-land-use/) data centers while limiting the input of communities and local tribes.
Critics of CEQA, signed in 1970 by then-Gov. Ronald Reagan, blame the law for hobbling home construction and driving housing and cost of living increases in California, which are among the highest in the nation.
Prop 45 will lower housing and utility costs by reducing “endless” bureaucratic delays and protect taxpayers by reducing waste and cost overruns, Yes on Prop 45 materials argue.
Yet there is no requirement in the measure to reduce housing costs or utility bills. And the nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=45&year=2026) estimates that Prop 45 could leave state and local governments paying $100 million or more a year, partly to cover fast-tracked projects’ environmental impacts.
“The housing issue is a smokescreen for all these other polluting projects,” said Little.
California passed laws last year that significantly streamlined CEQA by exempting (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billNavClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260AB130) urban and mixed-use housing construction from its provisions as well as certain infrastructure (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billNavClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260SB131) and clean energy (https://www.energy.ca.gov/programs-and-topics/topics/power-plants/opt-certification-program) projects.
“ I would hope that 100 percent of Californians would see this radical reshaping of California’s environmental law for the dangerous thing that it is. A wolf in sheep’s clothing.”
— Woody Little, No on Prop 45
None of the grassroots groups that promote “yes in my backyard,” or YIMBY (https://yimbyaction.org/), policies to build more housing and public transit in urban and suburban areas support Prop 45, Little said. Most are neutral, he said, while others oppose it.
Expanding housing beyond already developed areas means building new freeways, water connections and other expensive infrastructure that taxpayers ultimately pay for, Little said. And these projects often encroach on the wildland-urban interface, raising wildfire risk just as climate change is making fires more destructive.
At a time when California is already seeing the catastrophic costs of climate-fueled fires, Little said, the state should be requiring more environmental review around developments to assess and mitigate risk, not less.
What’s “Essential”?
Prop 45 covers nine types of “essential” projects, among them housing, water systems, clean energy (including carbon capture and storage), transportation, wildfire risk reduction and broadband internet access. All related and “ancillary” infrastructure is also covered.
Whether “ancillary” includes data centers, which typically require broadband infrastructure (https://tiaonline.org/how-broadband-workforce-development-and-standards-drive-data-center-growth/), has been a major point of contention.
Prop 45’s proponents have insisted the measure does not cover data centers, but legal experts disagree, pointing to $2 million in donations from just three data center builders and language buried in the measure’s 41 pages. Eligible projects include “broadband internet access projects,” defined as “mass-market retail service … that provides the capability to transmit data to, and receive data from, all or substantially all Internet endpoints,” a recent analysis (https://www.dailyjournal.com/articles/394431-prop-45-will-speed-data-center-construction) found.

That definition includes facilities that house the physical infrastructure used to transmit consumer data to and from the internet—which describes many data centers.
Yet data centers are conspicuously absent from the list of excluded controversial projects, which includes high-speed rail, the Delta Conveyance Project (https://www.deltaconveyanceproject.com/about-the-delta-conveyance-project), nuclear power and oil and gas facilities.
Inside Climate News asked the Yes on Prop 45 campaign why it sought to further limit environmental review after California had already significantly streamlined CEQA and why the measure does not explicitly exclude data centers. The campaign did not respond to multiple requests for comment.
California Resources Corp., the state’s largest (https://www.crc.com/news-releases/news-release-details/california-resources-corporation-completes-acquisition-crimson) oil and gas producer, has donated $500,000 directly to Prop 45 campaigns and another $500,000 (https://cal-access.sos.ca.gov/Campaign/Committees/Detail.aspx?id=1021742&session=2025&view=received) to a business committee sponsored by the California Chamber of Commerce. Oil and gas facilities are explicitly excluded from Prop 45, but CRC has a data center under environmental review at its Elk Hills oil field.
CRC did not respond to questions about whether it supports Prop 45 in order to fast-track its data center application.
Protecting Community Voices
“Proposition 45 would weaken CEQA protections for the very projects that still warrant careful scrutiny—development that could put people in harm’s way, fragment wildlife habitat, threaten water resources or damage irreplaceable cultural and sacred sites,” environmental and conservation leaders argued in a recent op-ed (https://lookout.co/california-has-already-streamlined-ceqa-proposition-45-goes-too-far/story).
One of the op-ed authors, Chris Wilmers, tracks mountain lions as lead researcher for the Santa Cruz Puma Project. In his study area, retaliatory killings for preying on domestic animals and vehicle strikes are the biggest threat (https://lookout.co/mountain-lions-ucsc-researcher-chris-wilmers-on-how-new-highway-17-animal-crossing-protects-santa-cruz-mountain-lions/story) to mountain lions as new housing and roads continue to encroach on the wide-ranging carnivores’ critical habitat.
An adult male mountain lion travels through a tunnel under Highway 101, heading south toward California’s Santa Monica Mountains in 2018. Credit: National Parks Service
CEQA requires developers to weigh alternatives to mitigate harm if new evidence emerges that a project would degrade critical wildlife corridors or endangered species’ habitat. But such facts would never come to light under Prop 45, which lets developers write their own rules, Wilmers and others say.
And the ballot measure strips away the rights of tribes that aren’t recognized by the federal government to safeguard their sacred lands.
That leaves large swaths of California, including the Central Coast, the San Francisco Bay Area and much of the Los Angeles area, without any tribal representation, said Noelle Chambers, executive director of the Amah Mutsun Land Trust.
Ethnographic studies conducted through CEQA consultations allowed the Amah Mutsun Tribal Band to protect burial grounds, artifacts and other sacred sites by stopping a proposed sand and gravel mine (https://openspacetrust.org/blog/sargent-ranch/) near Gilroy.
Prop 45 creates a “really harmful” legal precedent in the state by excluding non-federally recognized tribes from the process, Chambers said.
Julia Stein, deputy director of the Emmett Institute on Climate Change and the Environment at the University of California, Los Angeles, calls Prop 45 “a blunt force instrument” that is unlikely to build more projects faster by removing public participation.
It will cause a real loss of community engagement, she said, noting that CEQA is the only avenue for environmental justice communities to influence the environmental impacts of projects in their neighborhoods.
“We lived through a big infrastructure build-out in this country without laws like CEQA in the 1950s and ’60s, and we got environmental justice communities right next to freeways as a result,” Stein said.
CEQA has helped many communities (https://www.phi.org/thought-leadership/act-on-climate-california-communities-addressing-climate-change-and-health/) with elevated rates of asthma, cancer, heart disease and other ailments linked to industrial pollution limit additional harms in their neighborhoods.
A historically overburdened Latino community in southeast Los Angeles used a court order to compel a local government (https://legal-planet.org/2022/02/23/why-ceqa-is-a-useful-tool-for-environmental-justice-communities-in-california/) to review the risks of building an elementary school on a site contaminated with arsenic, and likely lead and asbestos, and require a cleanup. The mostly Latino residents of Riverside County’s Moreno Valley won an agreement to mitigate the harms (https://biologicaldiversity.org/programs/energy-justice/pdfs/WorldLogisticsCenter-Settlement-Agreement-20210429.pdf) on local air quality, climate and wildlife created by heavy-duty trucks serving a 40-million-square-foot warehouse.
Such mitigating measures might never have been identified, let alone required, if Prop 45 had been in effect, opponents say.
In addition to reducing the timeline for public agencies to review projects and fundamentally changing who can provide input, Prop 45 says only the developer or corporation can propose alternatives, said Mabel Tsang, political director for the California Environmental Justice Alliance, which opposes Prop 45.
“That takes away the strongest tool that communities like ours can use to protect ourselves from the worst health impacts before another polluting project is approved next door to our homes,” Tsang said.
Reagan, who signed CEQA as California governor but was known for accelerating deregulation as president, saw environmental protection as a nonpartisan issue. “Preservation of our environment is not a liberal or conservative challenge, it’s common sense,” he said during his 1984 State of the Union (https://www.reaganlibrary.gov/archives/speech/address-joint-session-congress-state-union-january-1984) address.
Now, on the heels of the Trump administration’s attempts to roll back the nation’s major environmental laws, experts say CEQA is more important than ever to safeguard public health and the environment from polluting industries.
Recent polling suggests that on Nov. 3, voters may not approve a measure designed to kneecap California’s most important air- and water-quality protection law.
A poll released Tuesday (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2026/) by the nonpartisan Public Policy Institute of California shows that 50 percent of voters oppose Prop 45, while those who support it dropped to 46 percent from 73 percent in July (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-the-environment-july-2026/), when voters knew only general information about the proposition.

Endorsement: CEQA is a mess. Prop 45 is even messier
Proposition 45 would significantly expedite the CEQA review process for eight categories of projects and potentially make it easier to build environmentally ruinous projects.
S.F. Chronicle illustration from Getty Images elements
By Chronicle Editorial Board (https://www.sfchronicle.com/author/editorial-board/) , Opinion Staff Oct 17, 2026
What’s the most polarizing four-letter word in California politics?
CEQA.
That wasn’t always the case. When then-Gov. Ronald Reagan signed the California Environmental Quality Act into law in 1970, the need could not have been more obvious. Californians were fed up with planners bulldozing low-income neighborhoods and communities of color for miles of polluting freeways. They were horrified by the ecological damage and habitat destruction caused by suburban sprawl. They were tired of top-down infrastructure projects that left communities feeling disempowered and voiceless.
CEQA laid out a basic protective framework: Before approving a project, government officials needed to evaluate potential negative environmental impacts and identify ways to mitigate or avoid them while providing ample opportunity for public review and input.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
But it didn’t take long for the law to be easily manipulated for ends that had little or nothing to do with the environment.
NIMBYs used the process to delay new infill housing — driving up costs and reducing the likelihood projects get built. Unions leveraged CEQA to extort favorable labor terms on projects (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/article/california-housing-union-labor-17802611.php). Courts showed a predisposition for allowing just about anything to become grounds for a CEQA challenge — which is how we ended up with a 2022 lawsuit against a UC Berkeley housing project (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/Editorial-UC-Berkeley-students-are-now-16931016.php) that effectively branded students as a form of pollution.
This editorial board has repeatedly decried CEQA abuses and has urged politicians to take decisive action (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/uc-berkeley-peoples-park-housing-ceqa-newsom-17816129.php).
In recent years, they have, to a degree.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
State lawmakers passed, and Gov. Gavin Newsom signed, bills to, among other things, permit more units on many single-family-home lots (https://www.sfchronicle.com/politics/article/California-cities-rush-to-limit-new-law-16647764.php), streamline the development of dense housing near transit (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/openforum/article/sb79-now-law-fight-affordable-housing-goes-21094908.php), exempt almost all infill housing from CEQA (https://sfchronicle.com/california/article/ceqa-housing-roadblocks-newsom-20402835.php) and speed up permitting timelines for large clean-energy projects (https://modelclimatelaws.org/resources/californias-sb-205-2022/).
But it’s still far too easy to bury certain essential projects in delay, litigation and costly uncertainty.
Proposition 45 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop45-text-proposed-laws.pdf), placed on the November ballot via signatures gathered by the California Chamber of Commerce, would significantly expedite the CEQA review process for eight categories of projects (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop45-110326.pdf) its authors deem “essential”: housing, water (other than the Delta tunnel (https://www.sfchronicle.com/news/article/will-california-ever-build-the-delta-tunnel-22237021.php)), clean energy (excepting nuclear power), healthcare, public safety, wildfire mitigation, broadband internet access, education and transportation (other than high-speed rail).
How would the measure aid these kinds of projects?
First, it establishes a litany of strict deadlines — some of which are technically already in CEQA but rarely enforced. Government agencies, for example, would have 30 days to determine whether a project application is complete, 365 days to conduct an environmental review and decide whether to certify it and 90 days to decide on permits. If agencies fail to meet these deadlines, applicants could trigger a public hearing within 60 days, at which time a final decision must be made. Applicants can sue if agencies don’t follow these procedures.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Prop 45 also significantly reduces paperwork. Government agencies could no longer repeatedly ask developers for more information to determine whether an application is complete — they would have one chance to produce an “exhaustive written corrections list.” Agencies would also be prohibited from changing the criteria or scope of their assessments mid-review. Agencies would no longer have to come up with multiple alternatives to environmentally impactful projects; instead, the applicant would propose just one alternative. The measure also restricts the public comments that can be included in the administrative record.
Finally, Prop 45 permits courts to halt only portions of a project determined to have “a specific, adverse impact upon public safety.” If courts sign off on an environmental review, no further lawsuits would be allowed. Lawsuits, including appeals, would need to be resolved within 270 days, with a possible 90-day extension.
In aggregate, these changes are far bigger in scope than any previous CEQA reform.
Some of the stipulations are eminently reasonable.
Enforcing deadlines is a no-brainer, as is eliminating excess paperwork and reducing frivolous litigation. Project applicants are not entitled to approvals, but they are entitled to decisions being made in a timely manner.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Furthermore, some of the projects Prop 45 seeks to streamline — like public transit, bike lanes and infill housing — are objectively good for the environment. They shouldn’t be subject to extreme CEQA scrutiny.
Others, however, are beyond questionable.
Prop 45 applies its streamlining process to freeway expansions and greenfield housing development in wildfire zones. And why does it specifically exempt the one transportation project that arguably needs the most help: California’s voter-approved high-speed rail, which is years behind schedule and billions over budget thanks in part to costly CEQA challenges? (https://grist.org/transportation/billions-spent-miles-to-go-the-story-of-californias-failure-to-build-high-speed-rail/)
Poll testing, said Emma Manoukian Chung, a strategist for the Yes on Prop 45 campaign. There was “voter appetite” for freeways and sprawl, but not high-speed rail.
But throwing a grab bag of poll-tested projects together and suggesting they should be evaluated on substantially similar terms is neither reasonable nor good policy.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Huge infrastructure projects — such as freeways and dams — have fundamentally different environmental impacts than infill housing. And infill housing has different environmental consequences than single-family homes in car-centric, high-wildfire-risk zones.
It makes no sense to apply the same scrutiny and deadlines to each.
It’s also unclear whether Prop 45 applies to data centers (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/article/data-centers-artificial-intelligence-dakotas-22362642.php). Opponents insist the “broadband internet access” category leaves open the possibility, while proponents insist that it doesn’t.
Ultimately, that question will likely have to be answered through litigation — ironically, the very thing Prop 45 is trying to curb.
It’s also ironic that Prop 45, despite aiming to reduce uncertainty, actually creates much more of it.
“This is deep, deep, deep in the weeds of environmental law,” Chris Elmendorf, a UC Davis law professor and one of California’s preeminent CEQA experts, told us. “It’s a super complicated body of law that they’re trying to change, trying to make it easier to build stuff.
“Some of the changes are good and some may be bad, and who knows what kind of second-order effects they will have?”
That’s why the state Legislature is best suited to handle complicated, nuanced policy, tweaking laws as needed — unlike the all-or-nothing blunt instrument of the ballot box.
“An initiative should be considered a last resort … when the Legislature is doing nothing,” Prop 45 opponent Darrell Steinberg, a former Sacramento mayor and state Senate leader, told us. But, he said, “just the opposite” is occurring.
We agree.
Lawmakers need to craft more fundamental CEQA reforms, particularly when it comes to housing, transportation and green energy projects. Some of those solutions are contained within Prop 45.
About Opinion

Its judgments are made independent of the news operation , which covers the news without consideration of our editorial positions.
But the measure as written would lock California into a regulatory regime that makes it easier to build the same environmentally ruinous projects that gave us CEQA in the first place.
Prop 45 is poll-tested political Swiss cheese, not a thoughtful effort to produce better outcomes. Vote no.
